topics.title: Overview and Classification of Corporate Strategies
explain: Strategies are formulated across Corporate, Business, and Functional management levels.
Corporate-level strategy provides top-down direction for the whole organization.
William Glueck and Lawrence Jauch identified four grand strategies: Stability, Expansion, Retrenchment, and Combination.
Strategies are categorized by organizational level, business life cycle stage, or competitive posture.
topics.example: A multi-business group sets corporate growth targets, while its electronics division designs competitive pricing, and marketing teams launch ads.
remember: The 4 grand corporate strategies are Stability, Expansion, Retrenchment, and Combination.
mistakes: Confusing generic corporate strategies by Glueck & Jauch with Porter's generic competitive strategies.

quiz.q: Which level of management is primarily responsible for formulating overall corporate strategy?
quiz.why: Top management makes corporate-level decisions to provide overall strategic direction to the firm.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Glueck and Jauch's four generic corporate strategies?
quiz.why: Focus Differentiation is a competitive strategy created by Michael Porter, not Glueck & Jauch.

topics.title: Stability Strategy
explain: The firm maintains its current business, product-market posture, and level of effort.
Focuses on incremental functional efficiency improvements rather than aggressive expansion.
Commonly adopted when products reach maturity or after rapid corporate expansion.
Startups rarely aim for stability because early-stage ventures require speed and agility to break even.

flow.title: Logic of Pursuing a Stability Strategy

topics.example: A long-established local bakery maintains its daily batch size and neighbourhood customer base without opening new stores.
remember: Stability strategy is NOT a 'do nothing' strategy; it requires ongoing incremental improvements.
mistakes: Assuming a stability strategy means zero effort, stagnant management, or zero growth.

quiz.q: Why do startup companies rarely adopt a stability strategy?
o: They require speed and agility to achieve early breakeven
They are required by law to diversify
They have excess financial cash reserves
quiz.why: Startups are in early stages and need rapid speed and agility to survive and reach breakeven.

quiz.q: Which feature best characterizes a stability strategy?
o: High risk and heavy capital investments
Maintaining status quo with incremental growth
quiz.why: Stability strategy focuses on maintaining current posture, safety, and incremental improvements.

topics.title: Internal Growth Strategies: Intensification, Diversification, and Innovation
explain: Expansion redefines business scope by significantly increasing investment and operational pace.
Intensification grows internally via Market Penetration (same market/product), Market Development (new market/same product), or Product Development (same market/new product).
Concentric Diversification (related) includes Vertical (Backward into inputs, Forward into distribution) and Horizontal (similar stage/competitors).
Conglomerate Diversification (unrelated) enters new fields with no common technology, process, or market links.
Innovation drives internal growth by solving complex problems, enhancing productivity, and building competitive advantage.

flow.title: Internal Growth Path Selection
steps: Apply related or unrelated growth tactics

topics.example: A coffee bean manufacturer merging with a coffee cafe chain executes forward vertical integration, while buying a paper mill is conglomerate diversification.
remember: Backward integration moves toward raw materials; Forward integration moves toward retail distribution.
mistakes: Confusing horizontal integration (same stage of production) with vertical integration (different stages in value chain).

quiz.q: A supermarket chain buying vegetable farms to secure supply is practicing:
quiz.why: Acquiring input suppliers upstream in the supply chain is backward vertical integration.

quiz.q: An EdTech company launching a luxury skincare brand is an example of:
quiz.why: Launching products in a completely unrelated market with no shared technology is conglomerate diversification.

topics.title: External Growth Strategies: Mergers, Acquisitions, and Strategic Alliances
explain: Merger combines two or more firms friendly into a single entity to expand operations and share profits.
Acquisition involves a financially stronger firm taking over and controlling a weaker firm, often forced.
Merger types include Horizontal (competitors), Vertical (supply chain), Co-generic (related field/tech), and Conglomerate (unrelated).
Strategic Alliance is a partnership where firms retain independent legal status while pooling resources.
Strategic alliances offer Organizational, Economic, Strategic, and Political advantages.
The major risk of an alliance is sharing trade secrets and potentially creating future competitors.

flow.title: Formation of a Strategic Alliance
steps: Pool technical, financial, or market resources

topics.example: A smartphone maker partnering with an AI software company to co-develop an operating system while both remain separate companies.
remember: Partner entities in a strategic alliance retain their separate, independent legal status.
mistakes: Assuming mergers and acquisitions are identical; mergers are friendly combinations, whereas acquisitions are takeovers.

quiz.q: When a refrigerator manufacturer merges with a kitchen appliance manufacturer, it is classified as a:
quiz.why: Co-generic mergers join firms in related markets or technology without being direct same-product competitors.

quiz.q: What is a major disadvantage of entering into a strategic alliance?
o: Risk of leakage of trade secrets to potential future rivals
quiz.why: Sharing resources and knowledge creates risks regarding trade secrets and potential future competition.

topics.title: Strategic Exits: Turnaround, Divestment, and Liquidation
explain: Strategic exits substantially reduce business activity scope to resolve operational or financial distress.
Turnaround Strategy is internal retrenchment focused on improving operational efficiency to reverse performance decline.
Danger signals prompting turnaround include negative cash flows, uncompetitive products, falling market share, and low morale.
The 5 Turnaround Stages: 1. Assessment of problems, 2. Situation analysis & strategic plan, 3. Emergency action plan, 4. Business restructuring, 5. Returning to normal.
Divestment Strategy involves selling or liquidating an SBU or division when turnaround fails or persistent losses threaten the firm.
Liquidation Strategy is the complete abandonment and legal closure of operations when all other options fail.

flow.title: Escalation Path of Strategic Exit Decisions
steps: Divest unprofitable SBU if turnaround fails
Liquidate total business as last resort

topics.example: A fitness app selling off its unprofitable regional diet section to focus on mainstream workouts executes a divestment strategy.
remember: Divestment is a constructive rehabilitation tool and should be viewed without business stigma.
mistakes: Believing turnaround strategy is only for bankrupt firms; it applies to any severe underperformance.

quiz.q: What is the first step in implementing a workable turnaround action plan?
o: Assessment of current problems and root causes
quiz.why: Stage 1 requires assessing current problems to diagnose root causes and the extent of damage.

quiz.q: Selling off an unviable business division after turnaround efforts fail is known as:
quiz.why: Divestment involves selling or liquidating a portion, division, or SBU of a business.

topics.title: Portfolio Analysis Models: Ansoff Matrix and ADL Matrix
explain: Portfolio models help multi-product firms allocate corporate resources to business units with high growth potential.
Ansoff's Growth Matrix pairs Products (Existing vs New) against Markets (Existing vs New).
Ansoff Quadrants: Market Penetration (Existing/Existing), Market Development (Existing Product/New Market), Product Development (New Product/Existing Market), Diversification (New/New).
Arthur D. Little (ADL) Matrix maps Stage of Industry Maturity (Embryonic, Growth, Mature, Ageing) against Competitive Position (Dominant, Strong, Favourable, Tenable, Weak).
ADL helps match strategic pushes (e.g., fast grow, differentiate, focus, retrench, withdraw) to business positioning.
topics.example: A domestic luxury clothing brand introducing its existing fashion range into overseas Asian markets executes Market Development.
remember: Diversification (New Product + New Market) carries the highest risk in Ansoff's Matrix.
mistakes: Misclassifying launching an existing product line in a new geographical territory as product development instead of market development.

quiz.q: In Ansoff's Matrix, introducing new modified products to existing current markets is called:
quiz.why: Product Development involves introducing new or modified products into existing markets.

quiz.q: The ADL Matrix evaluates strategic business units using which two criteria?
o: Market Growth Rate and Relative Market Share
Industry Maturity Stage and Competitive Position
Product Line Breadth and Net Profit Margin
quiz.why: ADL Matrix is based on 4 stages of Industry Maturity and 5 competitive positions.

topics.title: Portfolio Analysis Models: BCG Matrix and GE Nine-Cell Matrix
explain: BCG Growth-Share Matrix classifies SBUs using Market Growth Rate (Vertical) and Relative Market Share (Horizontal).
BCG Categories: Stars (High Growth, High Share), Cash Cows (Low Growth, High Share), Question Marks (High Growth, Low Share), Dogs (Low Growth, Low Share).
BCG Post-ID Strategies: Build (increase share), Hold (preserve share), Harvest (maximize cash), Divest (sell/liquidate).
GE Nine-Cell ('Stop-Light') Matrix evaluates units on Market Attractiveness (Vertical) and Business Strength (Horizontal).
GE Traffic Light Logic: Green = Invest/Expand (Go), Yellow = Select/Earn (Caution), Red = Harvest/Divest (Stop).

flow.title: BCG Matrix Portfolio Classification
steps: Plot SBU on Market Growth and Relative Share
Identify quadrant (Star, Cow, Question Mark, Dog)
Determine strategic posture (Build, Hold, Harvest, Divest)

topics.example: A company's well-established product with 60% market share in a mature, low-growth market reliably yields surplus cash flow as a Cash Cow.
remember: In the BCG Matrix, Stars naturally turn into Cash Cows as industry growth slows over time.
mistakes: Assuming a product with high market share is automatically a Cash Cow without verifying that industry growth is low.

quiz.q: In the BCG Matrix, business units operating in high-growth markets with low relative market share are called:
quiz.why: Question Marks have low relative market share in rapidly growing industries and need heavy cash investment.

quiz.q: In the General Electric (GE) Stop-Light Matrix, SBUs falling into the 'Red Zone' require which strategy?
quiz.why: Red zone cells represent low market attractiveness and weak business strength, calling for harvest or divestment.
